q: Which component receives routed staking rewards and mints service credits?

ev: They can be spent on gas, storage, or scheduled executions anywhere within the Rialo ecosystem.

ev: They are non-transferable outside the service context and cannot be speculated upon.

q: The SPM mints credits, maintaining a ____ backing against future RLO payouts.

q: What is Gauss?
a: A reconfiguration mechanism decoupled from consensus
A new DAG based consensus algorithm that replaces the one Rialo launched with
A zero knowledge proof system for verifying protocol upgrades
A fee market that prices validator rotation into and out of the active set
why: Gauss treats consensus as a modular component and keeps the reconfiguration mechanism stable while the consensus protocol changes.
ev: Gauss is a new reconfiguration mechanism that rethinks this approach. Instead of embedding reconfiguration logic within the consensus algorithm, Gauss separates reconfiguration from consensus

q: What is the difference between Gauss's inner log and outer log?
a: Inner: everything consensus orders; outer: only client transactions
The inner log is kept per validator; the outer log is the network wide view
The inner log stays private; the outer log is what light clients download
The inner log holds state roots; the outer log holds validator signatures
why: The inner log is the full consensus ordering including coordination messages; the outer log is the sanitized view of client transactions that execution sees.
ev: The inner log contains all entries ordered by consensus, including both client transactions and coordination messages. The outer log contains only client transactions

s: In Gauss the inner log is called dirty because it contains everything consensus orders, including coordination messages.
why: The dirty inner log carries everything consensus orders, while the outer log exposes only the consistent prefix execution should see.
ev: In this sense, the inner log is "dirty": it contains everything consensus orders, while the outer log exposes the consistent prefix of that ordering that execution should see.

q: What is the 'lie' in the title of the Gauss paper?
a: Not every entry committed by consensus reaches execution
Validators claim readiness before they have finished syncing their state
The old configuration only pretends to shut down and keeps ordering
Clients are told a transaction executed when it was quietly dropped
why: Consensus commits more than execution ever sees: coordination entries and post-handover entries from the old configuration are filtered out.
ev: This is the "lie" in the paper's title: not every entry ordered and committed by consensus is exposed to execution.

q: What are the three phases of a Gauss reconfiguration?
why: A Gauss transition replaces one epoch configuration with the next through preparation, handover and shutdown.
ev: Gauss performs these transitions in three phases: preparation , handover , and shutdown.

q: Which three coordination entries does Gauss define for reconfiguration?
why: EpochChange starts a transition, Ready signals a new validator is prepared, and Done carries the signed handover certificate; none are executed.
ev: Gauss defines three such entries: 𝗘𝗽𝗼𝗰𝗵𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲, 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆, and 𝗗𝗼𝗻𝗲. These entries appear in the inner log but are not executed.

q: Why does Gauss wait for every new validator's Ready message instead of just a quorum?
a: A validator could signal ready, then skip the new epoch, leaving it short of quorum
To give lagging clients enough time to resubmit their pending transactions
Because the handover certificate is only valid with every validator's signature
To let the old configuration finish ordering the blocks it has already started
why: Requiring all Ready messages avoids a faulty validator signalling readiness and then not participating, which could leave the new epoch stuck.
ev: This avoids a scenario where a faulty validator signals readiness but does not participate in the new epoch, leaving the system unable to reach quorum and make progress.

q: In Gauss, what marks the handover boundary h in the old inner log?
a: The position of the final Ready entry
The position of the EpochChange entry
The last entry before the epoch timer expires
why: The boundary is where the last Ready entry sits in the old inner log; it fixes the exact state the old configuration certifies and hands over.
ev: The boundary ℎ is the position of the final 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆 entry in the old inner log and defines the exact state that the old configuration certifies and transfers to the new configuration.

q: In the Gauss example, what happens to transactions T4 and T5 that the old configuration ordered after the boundary?
a: They are never executed and must be resubmitted in the new configuration
They are executed first in the new epoch, ahead of any new transactions
They are executed by the old configuration only and then reconciled later
They are merged into the new inner log automatically by the log sanitizer
why: Post-boundary entries from the old configuration are ignored by the log sanitizer, so T4 and T5 have to be resubmitted to the new epoch.
ev: T₄ and T₅ exist in the consensus-defined ordering, but the execution layer never sees them. Those transactions must be resubmitted under the new configuration

s: During a Gauss handover the old consensus instance must stop ordering transactions until the new configuration is active.
why: Gauss does not pause: the old instance keeps ordering during the transition, and execution in the new configuration simply ignores its post-boundary entries.
ev: This design enables fast handover between configurations without requiring the system to pause. The old consensus instance can continue ordering transactions during the transition

q: When can a validator in the old configuration safely stop participating in consensus?
a: After it sees a quorum of Done messages in the new configuration's consensus
As soon as it has submitted its own Done message to the new consensus instance
When the EpochChange entry is committed in the old inner log
After all Ready messages appear in the old inner log and the boundary is fixed
why: A quorum of Done messages means enough old validators agree on the boundary and can serve recovery, so the validator is no longer needed.
ev: Once a validator observes a quorum of 𝗗𝗼𝗻𝗲 messages, it knows it is no longer needed for recovery and can safely stop participating in consensus.

s: In the Gauss four validator example, the second transition is rejected with 2/4 signatures instead of the needed 3/4.
why: Only transition one reaches three Done messages; the honest validator in the quorum intersection refuses to sign conflicting handover certificates.
ev: the second transition is rejected because it does not have enough signatures (2/4 instead of 3/4)

q: Order the events of a Gauss handover as the post describes them.
steps: New validators submit Ready messages
The boundary h is fixed at the final Ready entry in the old inner log
The outer log starts following the new inner log at the boundary
Done messages from the old configuration certify the transition
why: Ready messages come first, the last one fixes the boundary h, execution follows the new inner log from there, and Done messages certify the handover later.
ev: The boundary ℎ is the position of the final 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆 entry in the old inner log and defines the exact state that the old configuration certifies and transfers to the new configuration. The outer log used by execution starts following the new inner log at the handover boundary, even though the transition is only certified complete later, when 𝗗𝗼𝗻𝗲 messages from the old configuration appear
context: Gauss moves the validator set from an old configuration to a new one without stopping the chain, using two logs: the validators' inner log and the public outer log.

q: Why does the Gauss post say upgrades are harder than they should be in many SMR systems?
a: Reconfiguration is tightly coupled to the consensus algorithm
Validators must all go offline at once to swap in the new binaries
Execution engines cannot be versioned without replaying the whole chain
Governance votes take too long to pass for routine parameter changes
why: When reconfiguration lives inside consensus, changing consensus changes reconfiguration too, forcing bespoke migrations and sometimes downtime.
ev: In many SMR implementations, the reconfiguration mechanism is tightly coupled to the underlying consensus algorithm. If the consensus algorithm changes, the reconfiguration mechanism changes too.

It is chosen by the participant with the lowest index
It is a hash of all published commitments
why: Adding all private polynomials gives an aggregate polynomial whose constant term is the sum of the participants' secret values, and that sum is the group secret.
ev: Because each participant's secret appears as the constant term of its own private polynomial, the constant term of the aggregate polynomial is the sum of those secret values

s: Each participant's final key share is the aggregate polynomial evaluated at that participant's own index.
why: Each participant adds up the intermediate shares it receives, which equals the aggregate polynomial at its index, so its final share is a share of the group secret.
ev: In general, each participant's final key share is 𝒙ᵢ = 𝒇(i). The intermediate share is a share of one participant's secret value; the final key share is a share of the group secret.

q: Which method does the post say participants use to recover the group secret from their key shares?
why: Lagrange interpolation rebuilds a polynomial from enough of its points, so t key shares recover the curve and its constant term, the secret.
ev: Participants recover the group secret from their key shares using Lagrange interpolation, which reconstructs a polynomial from sufficiently many of its points.

s: In the post's 3-of-5 reconstruction example using shares 1, 2 and 3, the Lagrange coefficients are 3, 3 and 1.
why: The coefficients in the example are 3, negative 3 and 1, giving f(0) = 3x₁ − 3x₂ + x₃, so the second coefficient is negative.
ev: if you use 𝒙₁, 𝒙₂, and 𝒙₃, then 𝒇(0) = 𝒙₁ · λ₁ + 𝒙₂ · λ₂ + 𝒙₃ · λ₃, with λ₁ = 3, λ₂ = −3, and λ₃ = 1

q: How does the post derive the group public key once the group secret s exists?
a: Y = gˢ, a fixed public base raised to the secret
Y = H(s), a hash of the secret
Y is the sum of each participant's own public key
Y is the first participant's polynomial evaluated at zero
why: The group public key is Y = gˢ with g a fixed public base element, and threshold signatures verify against this single Y.
ev: the protocol derives a corresponding group public key, Y = gˢ , where 𝑔 is a fixed public base element

s: A verifier can easily tell a threshold signature built from key shares apart from one made with a conventional private key.
why: The post says the opposite: the combined signature has the same form as a normal one, so to a verifier it is indistinguishable from a conventional signature.
ev: From the verifier's perspective, the signed data is indistinguishable from data signed by a conventional private key.

q: Order the four steps of the DKG simulation on Rialo Learn.
steps: Choose the number of participants and the threshold
Generate private polynomials
Distribute intermediate shares
Compute final key shares and derive the public key
why: The Rialo Learn simulation runs setup, polynomial generation, share distribution and then final share computation, with no trusted dealer at any point.
ev: the protocol executes in four steps: (i) choose the number of participants and threshold, (ii) generate private polynomials, (iii) distribute intermediate shares, and (iv) compute final key shares and derive the public key. There is no trusted dealer at any point in the process.
context: Distributed key generation lets several parties create one shared key without any of them holding the whole secret. Rialo Learn simulates it step by step.

q: Order the stages of the cross-chain stablecoin mint workflow described in the DKG post.
steps: The condition is met and the transaction is queued for execution
Destination chain payloads are derived from the original transaction
Validators sign each payload with their key shares
Partial signatures are combined into a threshold signature
A relayer or keeper delivers each payload to the destination chain
why: Once the condition holds, payloads are derived, signed by validator key shares into one threshold signature, and then relayed to the destination chains for execution.
ev: Once the condition is satisfied, the transaction is queued for execution. Payload generation and threshold signing : Transaction payloads for the destination chains are derived from the original transaction. Validators sign each payload with their key shares to produce partial signatures, which are then combined into a threshold signature. Delivery and execution : Each payload is delivered to the destination chain by a relayer or keeper.
context: A stablecoin is minted on another chain once a condition on Rialo holds. Validators sign the order together with a threshold signature, then it has to travel to the other chain.

q: What does Verifiable Secret Sharing add to the DKG process?
a: Public commitments to polynomial coefficients so received shares can be checked
A trusted dealer who audits every share
Encryption of every share under the group public key so only the quorum can read it
A slashing bond for each participant
why: With VSS, participants publish commitments to their polynomial coefficients, letting others check that the share they got matches what was committed.
ev: they also publish commitments to the coefficients of the polynomial they used to create those shares. Other participants can then check whether the share they received is actually consistent with what was publicly committed.

s: The post says vanilla secret sharing based on DKG principles can detect a participant who sends inconsistent shares.
why: Vanilla DKG assumes honest behavior and cannot detect or mitigate bad shares; that is why the post introduces Verifiable Secret Sharing.
ev: Vanilla secret sharing based on DKG principles assumes honest behavior and cannot detect or mitigate adversarial actions.

q: In the DKG post's stablecoin example, what role does Rialo play?
a: A hub whose master account controls accounts deployed on destination chains
A bridge that wraps the stablecoin and escrows collateral for every destination chain
The only chain allowed to mint the stablecoin
An oracle reporting the stablecoin's reserves
why: The stablecoin protocol uses Rialo as a coordination hub: a master account on Rialo controls remote accounts, including those that mint and burn.
ev: Suppose a stablecoin protocol uses Rialo as a hub to coordinate workflows across multiple blockchains. It has a master account on Rialo that controls other accounts deployed on destination chains, including accounts responsible for minting and burning.

q: Why does a prediction market need an oracle, according to the post?
a: The blockchain cannot observe the real world to learn what actually happened
To compute fair odds for each outcome
To custody the traders' collateral until the market closes and payouts are distributed
To match buy and sell orders quickly
why: A smart contract cannot read a news site or watch a Fed meeting, so an oracle has to import the real world fact that settles the market.
ev: a smart contract cannot read the Associated Press's website to know election outcomes, watch a Fed meeting to get the latest interest rate decision, or scan social media for product announcements. To settle predictions, the prediction market needs an oracle to report these facts.

q: Why do aggregation oracle quorums converge on stale values, per the post?
a: Reporting a fresh value that others lack risks slashing or penalties
Primary data sources publish too slowly for onchain settlement
Medians are only recomputed once a day
Reporters are paid per block rather than per update, so nobody bothers refreshing
why: Because the security model favors quorum agreement, a reporter who posts a fresh value nobody else has risks being slashed, so everyone settles on the stalest honest value.
ev: the quorum of reporters will logically converge on the stalest (honest) value in the quorum. For time sensitive values, reporting a fresh value that is unavailable to others risks slashing or penalization.

q: In an optimistic oracle, what happens to a reporter's bond after a successful challenge?
a: Part goes to the challenger and the rest is burned
It is returned after a cooling off period
It is split evenly among all token holders
It goes entirely to the protocol treasury, which then funds future challenger rewards
why: A successfully challenged reporter loses the bond: the challenger receives part of it and the remainder is burned.
ev: if someone successfully challenges, the original reporter loses their bond (part of it goes to the challenger while the rest is burned)

s: The post says optimistic oracles only work when another trusted source of information exists to reconcile disputes.
why: Optimistic oracles push the source of truth upstream, so they need some other trusted party, often governance, to settle disputes.
ev: Optimistic oracles function only when there is another trusted source of information to reconcile disputes.

q: Prophecy Markets opens a ____ dispute window for other participants to challenge a submission.
why: In the fictional Prophecy Markets example, submissions can be challenged for one day; if nobody objects, the result is finalized and payouts run.
ev: The system opens a one-day dispute window for other participants to challenge the submission; if no one objects, the result is finalized, and payouts are executed.

q: After the manipulated payout, how does Alice earn a second windfall in the Prophecy example?
a: She shorts Prophecy's governance token before confidence collapses
She sells her reporter bond at a premium
She buys the losing side of the market cheaply and waits for a second resolution
She claims the challenger's share of the bond
why: Knowing the lie will tank the market's reputation, Alice shorts the governance token and profits again when its price crashes.
ev: she opens a short position on Prophecy's governance token. When public confidence collapses, the token price crashes–giving her another windfall.

q: Which three quantities make up the post's informal condition for a profitable oracle attack?
a: Payout from false outcomes, short profit and token loss from the crash
Bond size, challenge window length and the number of reporters in the quorum
why: An attack pays when the false outcome payout plus the short profit exceeds the loss on tokens the attacker still holds when the price crashes.
ev: We can express this condition informally as: (payout from false outcomes + short profit) > (token loss from crash)

q: In the simulated example, Prophecy's governance token has a market capitalization of ____.
why: The simulation assumes a $500 million governance token, ten markets of $10 million each, 10% extractable per market and a 30% crash after an attack.
ev: Assume Prophecy's governance token has a market capitalization of $500 million. The protocol hosts ten active markets, each averaging $10 million in trading volume.

s: The Prophecy simulation assumes the governance token drops 50% after an integrity failure is discovered.
why: The simulation assumes a 30% drop in the governance token after an integrity failure, not 50%.
ev: Suppose an attacker can extract 10% of each market's volume if they falsify outcomes, and the governance token typically drops 30% following an integrity failure.

q: What governance participation does the post say Prophecy would need to restore security?
why: Even with 20% turnout the attack pays, so the post says Prophecy would need over 75% participation or much larger bonds, both impractical.
ev: To restore security, Prophecy would need far higher governance participation (> 75%) or larger bonds, both of which are impractical in real-world contexts.

q: How does a prediction market on Rialo resolve, according to the post?
a: A line of code points at a web source and trustlessly reports the result
A bonded reporter quorum votes on the outcome and gets slashed if wrong
Governance token holders settle every dispute
A median of several oracle feeds is taken
why: On Rialo the resolution is code pointing to a primary source such as nfl.com or federalreserve.gov, with no token vote or reporter quorum in between.
ev: the market's resolution is a line of code that can point to a source on the web, and trustlessly report the results

s: The post names nfl.com, federalreserve.gov and weather.com as example resolution sources for Rialo markets.
why: The post suggests nfl.com for a championship market, federalreserve.gov for rates and weather.com or ipcc.ch for climate.
ev: that might be nfl.com ; for rates, federalreserve.gov ; for climate, weather.com or ipcc.ch.

q: Why does the post say a failure in one Rialo market domain does not cascade into others?
a: Sources like the Fed, weather.com and NFL.com are unlikely to lie in coordination
Every Rialo market shares a single bonded quorum that governance can pause
Rialo halts every open market as soon as a dispute is raised in any one of them
Markets are resolved in a random order so an attacker cannot target one
why: Each market points to its own primary source, and it is far less likely that unrelated institutions coordinate to lie at the same time.
ev: it becomes even less likely to imagine they're coordinating with weather.com and NFL.com to all do so at the same time. Thus, even if the prediction market chooses the wrong resolution source, failure in one domain does not cascade across unrelated domains.

q: The post's third benefit is eliminating the middleman game of ____.
why: Every oracle gets its data from somewhere; Rialo makes that source explicit so there is no chain of middlemen passing the message along.
ev: Eliminating the middleman game of "Telephone". Every oracle gets its information from somewhere.

q: Compared to aggregation oracles, what can a Rialo app receive from a resolution source?
a: The full underlying data stream from a named publisher, not a median
Only a median of the reporters' values after outliers are pruned
A hashed commitment to the final outcome that is revealed after the challenge window
A probability instead of a binary result
why: Rialo can return the whole feed from a named publisher, so apps can compute their own medians or transforms without losing the extreme values.
ev: On Rialo, it's possible to return the full underlying data stream (e.g., a feed from a named publisher), not a median that prunes outliers.

s: Rialo secures prediction market resolution with its own bonded reporter quorum staked at the oracle level.
why: Rialo does not duplicate a proof of stake model at the oracle level; resolution pointers and results are finalized by the chain itself with no extra bonded quorum.
ev: Resolution pointers and results are finalized by the chain itself; there's no extra bonded reporter quorum to maintain.

s: The post says an MCP design on Rialo mitigates censorship at the routing layer.
why: To fake an outcome an attacker would need to corrupt or censor several visible institutions, and Rialo's MCP design mitigates censorship at the routing layer.
ev: On Rialo, an MCP design mitigates censorship at the routing layer, and protocol stake provides economies of scale

q: What question does the post say a Rialo app developer asks when picking a resolution source?
a: How likely is this primary source to misstate its own facts, and for how long?
Which token holders can be bribed most cheaply, and how many votes does that buy?
How large must the reporter bond be?
How many reporters are needed for a quorum?
why: Rialo reframes oracle security from a correlated governance risk into independent, verifiable ties to the public record, so the question is about the source itself.
ev: how likely is this primary source to misstate its own facts, and for how long? That reframes oracle security from a correlated governance risk into a set of independent, verifiable ties to the public record

q: What does Rialo Foundations I name as the deeper reason crypto apps are costly to build and run profitably?
a: Gas fees on the base layer
Scaling limits of first generation chains
why: The post says developers blame gas, scaling or friction, but the deeper issue is middleware costs stacking up across the stack.
ev: But there's another, deeper issue at play: the compounding cost of middleware.

q: Which term does the post say describes crypto's layered markups more accurately than double marginalization?
why: Because many monopolistic layers each add a markup, the post prefers compound marginalization over the textbook two layer term.
ev: While double marginalization is the original term, compound marginalization is a more accurate description of what happens in crypto.

q: What does the post call the 'crypto desert'?
a: A landscape of speculative financial tools with few useful non-financial apps
A period of low onchain volume and dead liquidity after a market crash
A chain that launched without any middleware ecosystem to support dapps
A testnet full of bots that never attracts real paying users
why: Compound marginalization selects for price insensitive users like whales and traders, so useful everyday apps never get built.
ev: It's no surprise, then, that we see a "crypto desert": a landscape dominated by speculative financial tools and a dearth of useful, non-financial applications.

q: The post says compounding middleware costs can erase up to what share of total economic surplus?
why: The post says compounding costs can wipe out up to 90% of surplus, leaving only high margin, price insensitive uses like leveraged DeFi.
ev: These costs can erase up to 90% of total economic surplus, leaving only high-margin, price-insensitive use cases–like leveraged DeFi–to survive.

q: What important side effect of Rialo's vertical integration does the post single out?
why: Collapsing several fee setting layers into one system lets pricing be set with total throughput and user welfare in mind.
ev: Rialo's vertical integration has an important side effect: pricing coordination.

q: Which persistent crypto dogma does the post say must be questioned to fix compound marginalization?
a: That base layers should do as little as possible
That tokens need inflation to secure the chain
why: The post argues blockchains should take on more of the functions developers already rely on instead of staying minimal.
ev: This calls for questioning one of crypto's most persistent dogmas (i.e., that base-layer blockchains should do as little as possible)

q: In the paper's lending example, an app that spends $1 on gas could incur how much in extra costs before a loan is liquidated?
why: Scheduling, data and indexing costs stack on top of the base fee, so $1 of gas can carry more than $5 of extra service costs.
ev: In the case of a lending protocol, an application that spends $1 on gas could incur over $5 in extra costs before the loan is successfully liquidated.

s: The post says lenders like Aave pay roughly 5% of each loan to liquidation bots.
why: The post uses this figure to show how middleware takes a cut: about 5% of each loan goes to liquidation bots.
ev: Additionally, lenders like Aave pay roughly 5% of each loan to liquidation bots.

s: The post puts Aave's average loan size at around $10,000.
why: The post says Aave's average loan is around $100,000, based on $9 billion borrowed across 90,000 monthly borrowers.
ev: Given that Aave's average loan size is around $100,000 (based on $9 billion in total borrows across 90,000 monthly borrowers), that translates to an extra $5,000 per liquidation in operational overhead.

s: The post describes today's layered fee extraction as a tragedy of the commons for pricing.
why: Each layer extracts rent from the same pool of users while assuming the others will moderate their fees, which the post calls a tragedy of the commons for pricing.
ev: Rialo is also designed to mitigate what we call a "tragedy of the commons for pricing." In the current ecosystem, each layer of infrastructure extracts rent from the same pool of users, assuming the others will moderate their fees.

q: In the paper's liquidation example the extra cost for scheduling was ____.
why: The breakdown is 300% extra for scheduling, 200% extra for data and $4,000 per month for indexing fast results.
ev: 300% extra for scheduling 200% extra for data $4,000 per month for indexing fast results

q: Formally, ____ is the value destroyed when uncoordinated pricing prevents mutually beneficial trade.
why: The post defines deadweight loss as pure waste from coordination failure that no user, developer or blockchain gains from.
ev: Formally, deadweight loss is the value destroyed when uncoordinated pricing prevents mutually beneficial trade.

q: What does Rialo call its framework for deciding which components get integrated into the protocol?
why: Rialo treats integration as an economic decision and calls the resulting philosophy supermodularity.
ev: At Rialo, we treat integration as an economic decision and adopt a systematic, quantitative framework that decides which components are integrated into the protocol and which remain external. We call this philosophy supermodularity.

q: Which real world example does the post use to show supermodularity creating new industries?
a: GPS, payments and phones merging into smartphones
Banks building their own ATM networks
why: Smartphones combined GPS, payments and phones, which unlocked ride hailing, logistics and e-commerce that none could enable alone.
ev: Initially, GPS, payment systems, and phones existed independently until smartphones came and combined all three functions into a single system.

q: Which chain does the post cite as an example of integrating price feeds and risk management with execution?
why: Hyperliquid started as a trading app and migrated to a chain that fused pricing, execution and liquidation into one engine.
ev: Hyperliquid is a great example: they started as a trading app and then migrated to a chain that integrated price feeds and risk-management primitives with execution.

q: What simple heuristic does the post give for designing supermodular systems?
a: Integrate the supermodulars and commoditize the complements
Integrate whatever lowers latency and fees the most
Externalize every data service and keep only execution native
Integrate only consensus, data availability and execution
why: Components that reinforce each other in production are integrated; everything else is bought as a commodity from external providers.
ev: This yields a simple heuristic for designing supermodular systems: integrate the supermodulars and commoditize the complements.

q: Which component does the post use as an example that complements execution in consumption but not in production?
why: A better fiat onramp makes the chain easier to use but does not make execution more capable, so Rialo treats it as a commodity.
ev: Fiat onramping is an example of a component that complements blockchain execution in consumption but not in production.

q: From which source did the Project 1337 demo ingest live trading data?
why: The demo pulled live trading data from Massive.io via an API call and preprocessed it inside a shielded computing environment.
ev: The demo required ingesting live trading data from Massive.io via an API call and running additional pre-processing

q: Which cross-chain workflow does the post give as an example of automation composed with native interoperability?
a: Mint WBTC to a Solana address whenever SOL:BTC falls below $X
Bridge ETH to Rialo whenever Ethereum gas drops below 10 gwei
Rebalance a Cosmos vault at every epoch boundary
Swap USDC to RLO whenever Rialo TVL doubles
why: Reactive transactions plus the native bridge and native oracles let a price condition on SOL:BTC trigger a cross-chain mint.
ev: This combination allows users to execute complex workflows like "Send 1000 USDC from my Rialo address to my Ethereum account" or "Send a request to mint WBTC to my Solana address whenever the SOL:BTC pair falls below $X".

s: The post treats weather data itself as a commodity but attestation of its provenance as a supermodular function.
why: Rialo integrates attestation and verifiable computation but sources the raw data, like weather from Weather.com, externally.
ev: The data itself (e.g., weather information) is often a commodity, and the costs of integrating data provision outweigh the benefits. But attesting to the provenance of data and performing confidential and verifiable computation using attested data are supermodular functions.

s: In Project 1337, raw stock price data was published onchain after being preprocessed.
why: Republishing raw data was barred by the Terms of Service, so only derived signals went onchain; raw price data never did.
ev: Raw price data never made it onchain in any way.

s: The post says Rialo's native bridge is run by a third-party relayer network.
why: The post says the bridge between Rialo and other chains is operated by the chain's own validator set.
ev: Interoperability is native to Rialo: users can transfer assets and send messages between Rialo and other chains via a bridge operated by the chain's validator set.

q: Combining reactive transactions with ____'s onchain gas funding mechanism enables recurring automated transactions.
why: Staking rewards converted into credits can fund an account's gas indefinitely, so scheduled operations never fail for lack of balance.
ev: Combining reactive transactions with Stake-for-Service's onchain gas funding mechanism enables Rialo to support recurring automated transactions that require minimal upkeep.

q: Put the steps of the post's authenticated bank transfer example in order.
steps: Validator decrypts the transaction
Validator calls the bank account with the authentication token
Balance is evaluated in a shielded computation environment
Transfer completes if the balance condition is met
Credential is erased and the outcome is posted onchain
why: The validator decrypts, calls the account, checks the balance inside shielded compute, transfers if allowed, then erases the credential and posts the result.
ev: The validator processing this transaction will decrypt it, make a call to the account using the authentication token, evaluate the balance in a shielded computation environment, and complete the transfer if the balance condition is met. Afterwards, the credential is erased from memory, and the outcome is posted onchain for verification
context: A transaction has to check a real bank balance before it pays out, without leaking the bank credential.

q: How does the post define system welfare?
a: Value created for developers and users net of execution, coordination and risk costs
Total fees collected by validators and middleware providers in an epoch
The sum of TVL and daily volume across all applications on the chain
The number of active addresses and transactions per day across the chain
why: High welfare means valuable onchain activity is cheap, reliable and scalable; fragmentation and rent extraction lower it.
ev: We define system welfare as the total value created for developers and users after accounting for execution costs, coordination overhead, and operational risk.

q: What does the post admit Rialo trades off by concentrating critical functions in the chain itself?
a: Some decentralization, for better pricing coordination
Finality speed, for lower execution fees
why: The post says concentrating control trades some decentralization for coordination and alignment in pricing and delivering services.
ev: Concentrating control of critical functions into one entity (the chain itself) trades off some decentralization for greater coordination and alignment in the pricing and delivery of execution and execution-adjacent services.

q: When fragmented liquidation costs approach the value of the liquidation, what two bad options does the post say protocols face?
a: Raise user fees or throttle liquidation frequency
Switch chains or shut the protocol down
Mint more tokens or borrow against the treasury
Lower collateral ratios or pause the oracle
why: Higher fees discourage usage while delayed liquidations let bad debt pile up, so users rationally exit either way.
ev: When this happens, protocols can either raise fees for users or throttle liquidation frequency.

q: Besides fees, which base layer guarantees does the post say middleware providers fail to match?
why: Stitching together bridges, oracles and privacy gadgets raises operational risk because those pieces can go offline, censor or get exploited.
ev: Middleware providers do not provide the same guarantees of availability, censorship resistance, and decentralization as the base layer.

s: The post claims integrated services on Rialo become free because their cost disappears into execution.
why: The post says the services do not automatically become free; the chain has pricing power but can offer them at a lower price.
ev: Those extra services don't automatically become free, but the chain has monopoly pricing power and can offer them at a lower price.

s: The post cites developer surveys showing protocol teams spend hundreds of thousands of dollars per month on offchain infrastructure.
why: Surveys cited in the post put monthly offchain infrastructure spend in the hundreds of thousands, worst on high throughput chains.
ev: Currently, developer surveys show that protocol teams are spending hundreds of thousands of dollars per month to integrate their applications with offchain infrastructure

s: The post says the integrated EV maker can cut prices yet earn higher margins because cheap products stimulate demand.
why: Lower prices grow demand, and at scale the manufacturer cuts unit costs, so overall profit rises despite the cheaper product.
ev: Reducing prices (counterintuitively) leads to higher margins because cheap products stimulate demand–as demand scales, the manufacturer can reduce unit production costs and make more profits overall.

s: The post argues a supermodular chain should integrate every service its applications need.
why: Integration only pays when components are strategically complementary; everything else is outsourced and treated as a commodity input.
ev: It is important to clarify that this doesn't mean a blockchain should integrate everything.

q: Vertical integration of complementary production components is the core insight of ____.
why: The post frames supermodularity as vertical integration applied to blockchains: bring complementary services into the protocol.
ev: Vertical integration of complementary production components is the core insight of supermodularity.

q: Order the Rialo liquidation loop described in the post.
steps: Native automation recalculates LTV ratios for open positions
A position falls below the threshold and the protocol emits an event
A reactive transaction responds to the emitted event
The chain automatically liquidates the loan
why: Native automation watches positions, the protocol emits an event when one falls below the threshold, and a reactive transaction liquidates it.
ev: Loan positions continuously monitored by native automation (set a transaction that recalculates LTV ratios for open borrowing positions at intervals or whenever oracle prices change) Undercollateralized loans automatically liquidated by the chain when collateral value is negative (set up the protocol to emit an event when the loan position falls below a threshold and create a reactive transaction that responds to the emitted event and automatically liquidates the loan)
context: A lending protocol must liquidate loans whose collateral falls too low. On Rialo the chain does the watching and the acting itself.

q: Which concurrency control approach does the post say Rialo uses?
why: The conclusion says a future post will cover how Rialo uses optimistic execution for a high performance execution environment.
ev: In the future, we will explore how Rialo uses optimistic execution to provide a high-performance execution environment for applications and guarantee the best possible experience for users.

q: In the naive parallel example ($100 balance, A subtracts $30, B adds $50), which final balance does the post say 'prints additional money'?
why: Both read $100; if B's $150 commit lands last it overwrites A's debit and creates money, while $70 landing last destroys money.
ev: The first (final balance: $150) prints additional money, while the second (final balance: $70) destroys money.

q: How do pessimistic execution systems pay the cost of not knowing whether transactions will conflict?
a: As higher fees on conflicting accounts
why: Pessimistic systems delay a transaction that could conflict, while optimistic systems pay later with re-execution.
ev: Pessimistic execution systems pay this cost upfront (before execution) in the form of delays–a transaction might be delayed if its execution could conflict with another transaction.

q: In the visualizer, which state and color mark a transaction being re-executed in optimistic mode?
why: Rerunning (orange) is the optimistic mode retry state; Waiting (gray) is the pessimistic mode delay state.
ev: Rerunning (orange): Transaction is being re-executed (optimistic mode)

q: Where does the post say the concurrency control dashboard can be accessed?
why: The post links the visualizer at concurrency-control.learn.rialo.io, where you can watch optimistic and pessimistic modes run.
ev: We've built a dashboard to visualize concurrency control that you can access at https://concurrency-control.learn.rialo.io/

q: With Exclusive Access ON, what happens to read-only Transaction C in the post's example?
a: It may wait and run sequentially despite only reading
It always runs concurrently with A and B
It is retried in optimistic mode
why: A scheduler that cannot tell reads from writes gives exclusive access per account, so even a pure read may be forced to wait.
ev: Transaction C will have to execute in sequential mode, even though it's only reading a shared account.

s: In the post's example, sequential execution always ends with a balance of $120 regardless of order.
why: Whether A or B runs first, the sequential result is $120, which is the benchmark parallel execution must match.
ev: No matter the order of execution, the final result is always $120.

s: The post says turning exclusive access off mostly boosts optimistic mode.
why: The boost is mostly limited to pessimistic mode; optimistic mode has no notion of exclusive access and already runs at maximum parallelism.
ev: The performance boost is mostly limited to pessimistic mode because optimistic mode doesn't have a notion of exclusive access and always permits maximum parallel execution and concurrent state access.

s: In the visualizer, Waiting transactions are shown in blue.
why: Waiting is gray and marks pessimistic mode delays; blue is the Executing state.
ev: Waiting (gray): Transaction is waiting to execute (pessimistic mode) Executing (blue): Transaction is executed

q: In pessimistic execution, conflicting transactions are grouped into ____ batches.
why: Transactions within a batch run concurrently while the batches themselves execute one after another.
ev: Conflicting transactions are grouped into conflict-free batches. Transactions within a batch execute concurrently, but the batches themselves are executed in a sequence.

q: Put the post's optimistic execution example in order, following Transaction A.
steps: Transactions A and B both read a balance of $100
Transaction B commits $150 before A finishes
Transaction A notices the state changed and discards its result
Transaction A re-executes with the new balance
The final result is $120
why: Optimistic execution lets both run, then validation catches A's stale read and reruns it against $150, giving the correct $120.
ev: Transaction A and B both read $100, but the balance reads $150 by the time Transaction A finishes (because Transaction B committed earlier). Transaction A notices the state change has changed, discards the old result, and re-executes with the new balance instead of overwriting it. The final result is $120 because Transaction A calculates $150 - $30 instead of $100 - $30.
context: Optimistic execution lets two transactions run at once on the same balance and sorts out the conflict afterwards. A and B both start from $100.

why: Reads can be stale and skip values, but they never move backward: the client sees K, then M, then Z and never J after K.
ev: A client connects to a lagging replica, and its first read returns "K." On a later read, the replica returns "M," and later still it returns "Z."

ev: The Domain Name System (DNS) is a real-world example of a replicated distributed system with eventual consistency guarantees.

q: Which consistency levels does the guide suggest for read-heavy blockchain workflows like querying historical chain data?
why: Block finalization needs strong consistency, but historical queries can relax to bounded staleness or eventual consistency for lower latency.
ev: while read-heavy workflows like querying historical chain data may use bounded staleness or eventual consistency to reduce coordination and improve latency

s: The guide says blockchains rely on strong consistency to prevent double spending.

ev: (for example, blockchains rely on strong consistency to prevent double-spending)

ev: The name reflects that the guarantee applies specifically to a client's own writes: read-my-writes does not guarantee visibility into another client's writes.

s: In the guide's eventual consistency example, no endpoint may return a balance of $130 because it was never written.
why: Eventual consistency allows stale reads but never invented ones; every value must come from a real committed write.
ev: In this example, no endpoint can return a balance such as $130 because it was never written.

q: Under ____, a client's view of committed writes only moves forward within a session.
why: Monotonic reads let the first read be stale but forbid the session from travelling backward in the write history.
ev: Under monotonic reads, a client's view of committed writes only moves forward.
